title: Irenaeus (c. 180)
hookLine: the glory of God is a human being fully alive

lines: A LETTER TO AN OLD FRIEND.
cards: An old friend has drifted into strange teachings, and a bishop writes to call him back. To make his point, he reaches for a memory. When I was a boy, he says, I heard Polycarp.
I can still tell you the place where he sat to teach, how he came and went, how he talked about John and the others who had seen the Lord. The bishop is Irenaeus, and Eusebius kept the letter.
After the martyrs of Lyon, the church there needs a new bishop. It gets this man, who carries Polycarp's voice in his head.

teach.b: Irenaeus wrote a long work that came to be called Against Heresies. First, what he was up against. Some teachers of his day said the material world was a mistake, made by a lesser power.
The body was a cage. Salvation was secret knowledge, handed to a few who were in on it. Second, his answer.

teach.h: ONE GOD MADE IT ALL GOOD.
teach.b: One God, he says, made heaven and earth, and made them good. The same God formed the human being from the earth, and the Son of God took real flesh. So the body isn't a prison to escape.
It's part of what God is saving. Third, the line.
In the Latin text it begins: Gloria enim Dei vivens homo. For the glory of God is a living human being. The Catechism of the Catholic Church gives it this way: the glory of God is man fully alive.
That's today's line. Fourth, the second half. The sentence keeps going: and the life of a human being is the vision of God.
Fully alive, for Irenaeus, isn't the same as busy, or impressive, or happy all the time.
It's a life turned toward God, seeing God, and made more human by it, not less. A God glorified by people being small and miserable wasn't the God Irenaeus knew. And notice when he wrote it.
Lyon had just lost its martyrs. Irenaeus didn't pretend life was easy.
Yet he wrote that God's glory looks like a person coming fully alive.

how: Catholics honor Saint Irenaeus as a bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his line on the glory of God is quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church in its teaching on creation.

o: the bishop of Lyon who heard Polycarp as a boy
the Roman governor who judged the Lyon martyrs
the first bishop of Rome to write in Latin

p: the bishop Irenaeus heard as a boy
the life of a human being
said the material world was a mistake

s: Irenaeus says the body is a prison to escape
he says one God made the world good, and the Son of God took real flesh.
he describes it in a letter to an old friend, kept by Eusebius.
the line about God's glory stops at fully alive
it goes on: the life of a human being is the vision of God.

games.q: you're the new bishop of Lyon. teachers are saying the world is a mistake and only secret knowledge saves. what do you do?
o: stay quiet and let it pass.
write a long answer: one God made it all good.
start a secret circle of your own.
games.why: Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies, insisting one God made heaven and earth, and that the flesh is part of what God saves.

practice: Feel your body for a moment: your feet, your hands, the air coming in, part of the good world, Irenaeus says, not a cage.

Then pick one ordinary thing ahead of you today, a meal, a walk, a conversation, washing a pan, and picture doing it with all of you there, no scrolling, no half-listening. If you pray, offer that one thing to God before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Irenaeus. The bishop of Lyon who heard Polycarp as a boy and said the glory of God is a human being fully alive. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a living human being — from Irenaeus's line Gloria enim Dei vivens homo.

carryVoice: Your line: fully alive. Not busier or more impressive, just more human. That's day seven hundred nine.
